explanations.answer: The words from the large scroll
explanations.explanation: The LORD tells Isaiah, “Name him Maher-shalal-hash-baz.” Those are the same words He told Isaiah to write on the scroll back in verse 1. So the message is on the scroll and in the nursery, and nobody can say they missed it.

Shear-jashub is a name from earlier in Isaiah. The LORD tells Isaiah to take along "your son Shear-jashub" when he goes to meet Ahaz (Isaiah 7:3). This new baby is a different story, and the LORD gives him a different name: Maher-shalal-hash-baz.

explanations.answer: The name of Ahaz king of Judah
explanations.explanation: Ahaz is the king of Judah the LORD sends Isaiah to speak to (Isaiah 7:3-4). But the LORD never asks for a baby named after him. His instruction is plain: “Name him Maher-shalal-hash-baz.” Naming a child after a trembling king would be a big ask anyway.

That's the word. The wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off by the king of Assyria. And the timing is the wild part: it all happens before the boy can say 'Father' or 'Mother.' I'd say that's a tight deadline.

I get the hopeful thought, but the LORD says the opposite. Nothing gets handed back here. The wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off by the king of Assyria. Once it's gone, it's gone.

Nice try, but nobody is tucking anything under a floorboard. The LORD says the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off, and the king of Assyria is the one doing the carrying. Hiding it would be like hiding a cookie jar from a toddler. It never works, and the text doesn't say it anyway.

Right, and it's a sad pairing. The LORD says this people rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah and rejoiced in Rezin and the son of Remaliah. Rezin is the king of Aram, and the son of Remaliah is Pekah, king of Israel (Isaiah 7:1). They turned down the gentle waters and cheered for those two instead.

It's actually true. The LORD says this people rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah and rejoiced in Rezin and the son of Remaliah. Rezin was king of Aram, and the son of Remaliah was Pekah, king of Israel (Isaiah 7:1). It's an easy one to doubt, since cheering for the very kings marching on you is a strange move.

explanations.answer: The mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates
explanations.explanation: Yes. The Lord says He will surely bring against them the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates. The people turned down the gentle waters, and now the waters get anything but gentle. Same theme of water, with a very different size.

Locusts are in the Bible, but they aren't in this passage. Here the Lord says He will bring the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates against this people. The picture stays on water the whole way through. Nobody in verse 7 is swatting bugs.

explanations.answer: A long famine in the land
explanations.explanation: No famine is mentioned in these verses. The Lord says He will surely bring the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates against them. The whole picture is a river leaving its place and covering the land. Nobody is going hungry in this verse.

Yes, the flood is a picture. The Lord says the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates are "the king of Assyria and all his pomp." So when the river overflows, think of a king and all his splendor coming across the land. The LORD hands us the meaning Himself.

It's true, and the verse spells it out. The Lord brings "the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates—the king of Assyria and all his pomp." The river stands for the king and everything he brings with him. So the flood isn't just weather, it's a picture of Assyria.

That's the one. The flood "will pour into Judah, swirling and sweeping over it, reaching up to the neck." Judah is the land where King Ahaz and his people live. The streams spread until they cover the whole land.

Egypt is a big river country, so I see the thinking. But this verse never mentions Egypt. The flood pours into Judah, and its spreading streams cover the entire land. Keep your eyes on the verse and the answer is right there.

Moab isn't in this passage at all. The flood pours into Judah, and its spreading streams cover the entire land. Judah is where Ahaz is king and where the trembling is happening. So the water's address is Judah.

Yes. The message says, "prepare for battle, and be shattered; prepare for battle, and be shattered!" Huddling, listening and getting ready all end in the same word. The peoples can't line up their troops fast enough to change it.

That's a nice thought, but the message says the opposite. The peoples huddle together and prepare for battle, and the text says they will be shattered. It says it more than once, so there's no room for a win. If anything, this is the loudest 'no' in the passage.

No reward here, I'm afraid. The peoples are told to huddle together, pay attention and prepare for battle, and then comes the word "shattered." Getting ready for a fight doesn't change the ending. A prize basket never shows up in these verses.

It's the other way around. The message says, "Devise a plan, but it will be thwarted; state a proposal, but it will not happen." The plan gets blocked and the proposal does not happen. That's one stubborn "but" in each half of the verse.

Right. The text says, "Devise a plan, but it will be thwarted; state a proposal, but it will not happen." People can plan all they want, but the plan is thwarted and the proposal doesn't happen. Not one clipboard in the land can change that.

That's the reason, and it's the last line of the passage: "For God is with us." The plans fall apart because God is with His people, not because anyone else got clever. It's a good note to end on after all that flooding and shattering.

explanations.answer: For their kings are too weak
explanations.explanation: The message never says the kings are weak. The reason it gives is "For God is with us." Reading it that way shifts the focus from the kings to the One who is with His people. Their strength isn't the question here.
Assyria isn't guarding anything in this passage. Earlier, the king of Assyria is the flood that sweeps over Judah. The reason for the thwarted plans comes at the very end: "For God is with us."
